clue.text: Place for cutting and getting first slice of bread with jam — Henry's tucking in!

indicators.note: Henry is tucked into the word for getting, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: copping is slang for getting or catching
H is the symbol of the henry, the unit of inductance

indicators.note: the first slice of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: to jam a door or wheel is to lock it

explanation.surface: A kitchen scene: bread and jam being sliced while a man called Henry tucks into his share.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tucking in' puts H inside COPPING (slang for getting) to make CHOPPING; 'first slice of' takes B from 'bread', and 'jam' gives LOCK.
explanation.definitionFit: A butcher's or cook's wooden board where meat and vegetables are chopped is a place for cutting.

clue.text: Down Clumsy fellow made this ineptly

indicators.note: done ineptly, the letters are bungled into a new order

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fellow, as in FRS
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A clumsy man botched the job he made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down' is the column heading picked up from the printed page, not part of the clue. 'ineptly' shuffles F (fellow) with MADE and THIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Ham-fisted is an informal adjective for awkward or bungling with the hands, a synonym of clumsy.

clue.text: Annoy woman with exercises

parts.note: PE is physical education, school exercises
Eve, the first woman in Genesis

explanation.surface: Someone irritates a woman by making her do workouts.
explanation.definitionFit: To peeve someone is to irritate them, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Wrong — one town closing down yard is wrong

parts.note: ill as in ill-gotten or ill-advised means wrong or bad
I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: the yard is shut out at the end of the word, as a business closing down stops

parts.note: a city is a large town

explanation.surface: A complaint that shutting a town's yard was a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue begins and ends with 'wrong': the first supplies ILL, the last is the definition. 'closing down' removes Y (yard) from CITY to leave CIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Something illicit is forbidden by law or custom, so it is unlawful or improper.

clue.text: Buy your own tulips!

parts.note: read as an instruction to pay your own share, with tulips hinting at the Netherlands, where the flowers are famous

explanation.surface: A gruff instruction to a guest to buy their own flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: Tulips are the national emblem of the Netherlands, so buying them is acting Dutch; the phrase for each person paying their own share uses that nationality.
explanation.definitionFit: Going Dutch means each person in a group pays for themselves, as when everyone buys their own.

clue.text: Plant producing yellow ointment?

parts.note: lemon is a pale yellow colour
a balm is a soothing ointment

explanation.surface: A question whether some plant yields a yellow skin cream.
explanation.definitionFit: Lemon balm is a lemon-scented herb of the mint family, so it is a plant.

clue.text: Sounded unhappy about journey, we hear

indicators.note: we hear tells us the letters are judged by how they sound when spoken

parts.note: about gives C (circa) and a journey is a ride, run together as one sound

explanation.surface: Someone moaned about a trip, according to reports.
explanation.walkthrough: C (circa, about) followed by RIDE (journey) is pronounced like the answer, signalled by 'we hear'.
explanation.definitionFit: To have cried is to have wept or made a sound of distress, so it is sounding unhappy.

clue.text: High-level station -odds on one place where trains arrive?

parts.note: SP is starting price, the betting odds on a horse
an ace is a one in a pack of cards
a platform is where passengers meet incoming trains

explanation.surface: A betting tip on a railway station, odds offered on one platform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High-level' means far above the earth, not senior. SP (starting price, the odds at a British race meeting) sits on ACE.
explanation.definitionFit: An orbiting space station is a station at a very great height, a platform for living in space.

clue.text: More than one theatre worker shows astonishment about a star turning up

indicators.note: the astonished word wraps around the other piece

parts.note: to stagger is to reel in amazement

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up reads the phrase a star backwards

parts.note: a big name is a celebrity, a star

explanation.surface: Someone is amazed when a celebrity arrives at the theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning up' reverses A NAME to EMANA, which 'about' puts inside STAGGERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Stage managers run the backstage side of a production, so they are plural theatre staff.

clue.text: Me, with lump pulsing, directed to be beaten

indicators.note: pulsing suggests throbbing movement, so these letters jump into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
led means guided or directed

explanation.surface: A throbbing bruise sends someone to be thrashed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pulsing' rearranges ME and LUMP to make PUMMEL, followed by LED.
explanation.definitionFit: Pummelled means struck repeatedly with fists, a synonym of thrashed.

clue.text: Majority around island affected by water

indicators.note: the word for majority goes around the island letter

parts.note: most means the greater part, the majority

explanation.surface: Most of an island is waterlogged.
explanation.definitionFit: Moist means slightly wet or damp, the state of something touched by water.

clue.text: Right, I'm breaking into church — producing this?

definitions.text: Right, I'm breaking into church — producing this?

indicators.note: breaking into puts the right-and-I'm letters inside the church letters

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A burglar announces a break-in at a church and asks what offence that is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaking into' puts R and IM inside CE. As a whole, breaking into a church is an offence against the law.
explanation.definitionFit: Breaking into a church is burglary, an offence against the law.

clue.text: It's a singular deluge that's this scrappy!

definitions.text: It's a singular deluge that's this scrappy!

parts.words: It's a singular deluge that's this scrappy!
parts.note: a heavy downpour is said to rain household pets of two kinds in the plural; make them singular and the phrase describes fierce quarrelling

explanation.surface: A remark that one particular flood is oddly fragmented.
explanation.walkthrough: Heavy rain 'rains cats and dogs'; 'singular' reduces both animals to one each, and that hyphenated form describes fighting, since cats and dogs famously squabble.
explanation.definitionFit: A cat-and-dog life or fight is constantly quarrelsome, and scrappy means given to fighting.

clue.text: Casual attack in which drug's stolen

parts.note: pot is slang for cannabis, with the possessive s
hot is slang for stolen goods

explanation.surface: An opportunistic raid during which some narcotics go missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as 'pot's hot': the drug is stolen.
explanation.definitionFit: A pot shot is a random, carelessly aimed shot, so a casual attack.

clue.text: Difficult ship, one refusing to diverge from chosen course

definitions.text: one refusing to diverge from chosen course

parts.note: hard means difficult
a liner is a large passenger ship

explanation.surface: A stubborn vessel that will not leave its set route.
explanation.definitionFit: A hardliner sticks rigidly to a policy and will not compromise, never leaving the chosen path.

clue.text: A Mahler broadcast from a Dutch town

indicators.note: broadcast also means scattered, as seed is sown, so these letters are scattered

parts.note: taken as written
the composer's name taken as written

explanation.surface: A Mahler symphony is aired from the Netherlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Haarlem is a city in North Holland, the capital of that province, so a Dutch town.

clue.text: Pronunciation defect in all alto trills

indicators.note: a trill quivers between notes, so these letters are shaken into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A singer's speech problem shows in every trill the altos sing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trills' looks like part of the singing picture but signals the anagram of IN, ALL and ALTO.
explanation.definitionFit: Lallation is the faulty pronunciation of r as l, a speech impediment.

clue.text: Girl heading off to embrace the men in the country

indicators.note: the shortened name embraces the soldiers, holding them inside
heading off removes the first letter, the head of the name

parts.note: Sandra is a girl's name
OR is other ranks, ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: A girl leaves to hug the men in her homeland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading off' cuts S from SANDRA to leave ANDRA, which 'to embrace' wraps around OR (other ranks).
explanation.definitionFit: Andorra is a small independent principality in the Pyrenees, so a country.

clue.text: Girl to show evidence of existence in chronicle

indicators.note: the existing verb sits inside the record

parts.note: an annal is a yearly record, a chronicle
to be is to exist

explanation.surface: A girl appears in a history book to prove she was real.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts BE (exist) inside ANNAL, a year's chronicle.
explanation.definitionFit: Annabel is a female first name, so a girl.

clue.text: Exotic set of instruments — something played, by the way (not English)

parts.note: a game is something one plays

indicators.note: the English letter E is dropped from the word for way

parts.note: a lane is a narrow way or road

explanation.surface: A traveller hears foreign instruments by the roadside, not English ones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not English' removes E from LANE to give LAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A gamelan is an Indonesian ensemble of gongs and metallophones, so an exotic orchestra.

clue.text: Good girl and man taken up from Hell

indicators.note: in a down clue, taken up reads the girl and man upwards, backwards

parts.note: Anne is a girl's name
he is the male pronoun

explanation.surface: A good girl and her man are rescued from the underworld.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken up' reverses ANNE + HE to EHENNA, after G.
explanation.definitionFit: Gehenna is the place of torment in Jewish and Christian scripture, a name for Hell.

clue.text: Non-existent meal?

parts.note: alludes to the saying that there is no such thing as a meal given for nothing

explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'there's no such thing as a free lunch' means nothing truly comes for nothing, so this midday meal is the one that does not exist.
explanation.definitionFit: Proverbially nobody gets food without paying somehow, so a meal costing nothing is a fiction.

clue.text: Be glum, turning up around end of races -here?

indicators.note: the reversed word goes around the final letter
in a down clue, turning up reads the glum verb backwards

parts.note: to mope is to be glum

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: A punter sulks at the end of the racing at this place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning up' reverses MOPE to EPOM; 'around' wraps it round S, the 'end of races'. Epsom Downs is a famous English racecourse, home of the Derby.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsom Downs in Surrey hosts the Derby, so it is a place where races end.

clue.text: Name adopted by girls retorting in colloquial speech

indicators.note: the name letter is taken into the reversed girls word
to retort is to turn back, so the girls word is read backwards

parts.note: gals is informal for girls

explanation.surface: Girls answer back with a nickname in street talk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retorting' reverses GALS to SLAG, and 'adopted by' puts N inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang is informal vocabulary used in everyday conversation, so colloquial language.

clue.text: Brief attempt to secure runs

indicators.note: the attempt holds the runs letter firmly inside

parts.note: a shot is an attempt, as in have a shot
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A quick try to score some runs at cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Short means lasting a little time, a synonym of brief.

clue.text: Gum concealed by dentures — ingenious!

indicators.note: concealed by says the answer lies inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Chewing gum stuck in false teeth, a clever idea.
explanation.definitionFit: Resin is the sticky substance exuded by trees, which is also called gum.

clue.text: Store of ammunition -rig's abandoned by brigand or thrown around position on ground

indicators.note: abandoned by means the following words drop those letters

parts.note: taken as written
the word rig, its possessive s ignored, is the run of letters removed

indicators.note: thrown around means the remaining letters are flung round the next piece

parts.note: taken as written
the lie of a golf ball is its position on the ground

explanation.surface: A bandit discards his gear around a camp, ammunition belt and all.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking RIG out of BRIGAND OR leaves BANDOR, which 'thrown around' wraps round LIE (a ball's lie in golf).
explanation.definitionFit: A bandolier is a shoulder belt with pockets for cartridges, so it holds ammunition.

clue.text: Item of furniture redesigned at Slumberland

indicators.note: redesigned says the letters are reworked into a different arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
a brand of beds, taken as written

explanation.surface: A piece of furniture gets a makeover at a bed maker.
explanation.walkthrough: Slumberland is a British bed brand; 'redesigned' rearranges AT SLUMBERLAND.
explanation.definitionFit: An umbrella stand is a hallway holder for umbrellas, a piece of household furniture.
